newsitem.title: GERMANY: Flood-hit E.German farmers count losses.
newsitem.headline: Flood-hit E.German farmers count losses.

text.p: Farmers in flood-threatened areas of eastern Germany's Brandenburg state face losses of hundreds of millions of marks, a spokesman for the state's agriculture ministry said on Monday.
At risk are up to 76,165 hectares of farmland in four districts, of which 64,388 ha are arable area.
They include 41,332 ha of grain, 5,486 ha of oilseeds and 2,331 ha of sugarbeet.
The area also has 60,789 farm animals.
"Damage to farms and crops is already extensive...the losses will take at least two years to overcome," said spokesman Jens-Uwe Schade from his base in Potsdam near Berlin.
"That is on the basis of current damage and rules out the worst-case scenario, under which dikes would burst to flood the entire Oderbruch region."
Dikes resisted the pressure of the swollen Oder river overnight but more water was expected over the next few days, possibly leading to the evacuation of up to 24 villages.
Germany has so far escaped the worst of the floods in Europe, which have claimed lives in Poland and the Czech republic.
But Schade said farmers who seven years after unification were still struggling financially had incurred heavy costs when they evacuated and left behind some of their livestock.
Crops harvested in a hurry would not yield their full potential and emergency sales might not bring the expected profits.
Expensive machinery and silos were also under threat.
The farm ministry would provide some storage space so that farmers did not have to sell crops at rock-bottom prices.
While the threatened region is small when compared with Germany's total grain area of 7.04 million ha, individual farmers face disaster.
Schade knew of one formerly collective farm near Wiesenau south of Eisenhuettenstadt where 7,000 hectares of arable land became inaccessible when the Oder overflowed its banks.
Bonn agriculture minister Jochen Borchert was expected in the area on Monday and farmers were looking to secure a waiver in land-lease payments arranged after unification in 1990.
Banks and insurance companies would be asked for support when it came to loan payments.
The Potsdam ministry would seek federal aid and permission to channel structural aid granted to the Brandenburg state as a whole into the flood-hit areas.
Credits of more than 200 million marks promised by Chancellor Helmut Kohl to the flood-hit regions from state-owned KfW bank should be extended to include agriculture.
Borchert would be asked to apply for European Union aid.
